utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon, everybody. Good afternoon to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-54-R77.5-PT, the case against Florence Hartmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Shall we start with representations. Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I appear on behalf of the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I appear on behalf of the Prosecution this afternoon and with me is Lori Ann Wanlin, also of Canada.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If it please Your Honours, Mr. President, good afternoon. My name is Karim Khan. I appear for Florence Hartmann along with co-counsel Guenal Mettraux and our legal assistant Arina Koligina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan and Mr. Mettraux. You are most welcomed. It's the first time you are appearing in this case, and, therefore, it's my duty to welcome you as well as your legal assistant, of course. Good afternoon, everybody. The reason why we decided to be, the three of us here, present for this Status Conference is that the trial is practically round the corner. It's a matter of days. So there is no point in having just me presiding over the Status Conference, then going back to my colleagues and possibly having to come back to you, so we decided to proceed this way. This is the first Status Conference of its kind in this case, and just for formality's sake but also for public consumption, I just wish to underline that such Status Conferences are held pursuant to Rule 65 bis (a) of the rules, and the purpose of a Status Conference is to organise exchanges between the parties so as to ensure an expeditious preparation for trial; and, secondly, to review the status of the case and to give an opportunity to the accused to raise issues, including personal issues like physical condition and health -- health matters, which I hope do not exist in this case where an accused is not in custody. In preparation for the trial, you will recall that on the 8th of January of this year, the Amicus Prosecutor - and I will be referring to him henceforth as the Prosecutor - filed his pre-trial brief; and seven days later on the 15th of January, the Defence filed theirs. As you are aware, trial is scheduled for next week, namely, the 5th and the 6th of February, with a Pre-Trial Conference to precede immediately the commencement of the trial. Since we last met and until basically yesterday, we have had a long series of motions, most of which have been decided. In particular, I'm referring to the more recent ones. I don't know if you wish -- perhaps want to give an indication to the Trial Chamber of what your intentions are, Mr. Khan? I'm talking of the ones that have already been decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's our intention to seek certification under Rule 73 for leave to appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. That is what we expected, in any case, but we'll come to that matter in due course, about certification. There are three outstanding motions which we will be dealing very briefly with. I'll tell you beforehand what our approach is going to be. These three motions are going to be decided orally today. One of them will give you a very short oral reasoning and that will be it, and then, of course, you can seek certification later. The other two will be decided orally today with written reasons to follow at the earliest, and that means very early in the coming week. So let me go through them one by one. The first one is a Prosecution motion to amend its 65 ter list. This was filed, as you will recall, on the 20th of January, 2009. Now, it hasn't been decided, but if you've read carefully yesterday's decision regarding your motion on the taking and disclosing of proposed witness statements, you would have noticed that in a somewhat unorthodox and direct fashion, we did make it clear what our position would be. However, things being what they are, that is, that it has not yet been formally decided, and since, Mr. Khan, you have not yet responded to this motion which now shouldn't present any particular difficulties, I would like you to tell us if you wish to respond orally to it now so that we can proceed with our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm most grateful for the kind invitation. Your Honours can proceed to render your judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and thank you for being practical, Mr. Khan. This is usually much appreciated by the Trial Chamber. We, yesterday, stated in paragraph 9, if I recall well, of our decision the following: "Finally, on the 20th of January, 2009, the amicus filed the Prosecution motion to amend Rule 65 ter witness and exhibit lists, wherein the amicus clarified that he intends to reduce the scope of the expected testimony of Mr. Ruxton. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the clarification made by the amicus in this motion meets the concerns of the Defence as raised in its addendum and adequately puts the Defence on notice of Mr. Ruxton's expected testimony." Now, on the basis of that, we believe that there is no reason why the Prosecution motion to amend its 65 ter list should not be accepted, and more or less for the same reasons we are granting the motion. And if you will seek certification, we will tell you what the procedure is going to be later on. The next Defence motion is a much more substantial motion, and it's only yesterday that we received the response from the Prosecutor, and we have been working intensively on it. Beyond that, we have also met, made our considerations after long deliberations. We just finished, actually, a short while ago, and we have come to a conclusion to deny the motion. We will be following with a written decision in the course of next week, Monday or Tuesday, and you will know the basis for our decision and on which you can then base your request for certification, if you still intend to proceed that way. The third one is an urgent Defence motion for the issuance of a subpoena to amicus curiae Prosecutor, Mr. Bruce MacFarlane, pursuant to Rule 54. You are definitely aware, Defence certainly even more than Prosecutor, that this motion was predicated on a situation assuming that the decisions that we handed down up to yesterday were not handed -- were not decided as yet, were not taken as yet. They have now been taken. In other words, you had made it clear that you would have preferred to interview Mr. MacFarlane prior to the taking of that decision, of those decisions. In light of the fact that Mr. MacFarlane indicated that he would only consider your request to be allowed to be interviewed after that certain motions had been decided, we considered that. Now, the motion itself for the subpoena to be issued to the amicus curiae can be decided today, and we are denying the motion, and reasons will follow in the coming week, either Monday or Tuesday. On the assumption that everything goes smoothly, and according to the law, the intention is to start the trial as scheduled on Thursday of next week. Like every other trial, I would have expected, and I am sure it did happen, the usual -- for the usual exchanges between the parties to have taken place and also been mutually concluded to mutual satisfaction. I understand that in the course of these exchanges there may have been some problems. If these problems are still existing, then I would like you to speak out now. If they have all been sorted out, then perhaps you can enter a declaration to that effect for the record. I think I will start with you, Mr. Khan. Do you still have any outstanding problem with Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, with Mr. MacFarlane personally, no, not at all. I don't know him. I haven't had the pleasure. As far as his investigation is concerned and the material that has been provided to the Defence, we have very significant and grave misgivings about our ability to do the job that we are entrusted to do, which is to properly represent our client. Your Honours, you have ruled just now on the issue of the subpoena, but there were a number of other matters that have yet to be decided. My learned friend provided us with a list of suggested agreed facts. We gave our response sometime ago, more than a week, anyway. In addition, I received an e-mail only today from my learned friend which was in response to some further suggested agreed facts proposed by the Defence, and in that e-mail - he will correct me if I'm wrong - he states that they seem at first blush to be potentially agreeable, but he wants time to consider them. So, Your Honour, those are matters which are yet to be decided between the parties. We have also asked for evidence regarding the provenance of certain documents regarding the chain of custody. The position of my learned friends up to this point has been to deny that. He has not provided us information as to the provenance of certain documents. Now, Your Honours, one of the very real difficulties that we face, and this was the focus of our subpoena motion, is that my learned friend wears two hats. He appears robed today in court, but in a previous incarnation, he had the privilege of being appointed the amicus investigator, and the only way we as a Defence team can look at the skull beneath the skin, the only way we can pierce the process of this investigation, is to ask the investigating officer, who is sitting opposite me, certain questions. Your Honours, we have nobody else to ask regarding the provenance of documents. We have nobody else to speak to regarding the conduct of investigations. So these were some of the serious misgivings that I raise for the record. Of course, in due course we will seek certification for leave to appeal on a raft of motions that Your Honours have graciously decided. But, Your Honours, these are matters which give the Defence serious cause for concern about the fairness of this process. Your Honour, there is, of course, a fundamental difference between the Defence and the Prosecution. It is our respectful submission that in order to arrive at a satisfactory conclusion, a just result, one must -- and Your Honours, alive to your oaths and Rule 13, with all the wealth of experience you bring, will want to pay close regard to the process itself. It can't be glossed over. Due process has a hallowed place in international law and in domestic law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not discuss matters that are pleasures yet to come, so to say. But for the time being, I ask you to limit yourself to whether the exchanges that one would have expected to have been concluded by now, would the Prosecutor have been concluded or not. I understand that some of them are pending, and I will intervene as soon as you finish stating other matters, other possible pending issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my learned friend has responded on time to our requests. I think we have tried to respond on time to his. There is communication, of course. Neither party often gets everything it wants. Sometimes they do, but not always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And the other thing I wanted to mention, Mr. Khan, is that previously you would have certainly noticed that prior to deciding the last of the three motions, namely, the subpoena one, I did point out that Mr. MacFarlane had never refused outright your request but said that he would consider the issue after the motions he refers to had been decided. So I would suggest that you try to approach Mr. MacFarlane, and maybe he wishes to address the Trial Chamber on this and also any outstanding matters with the Defence now. Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful, and we will definitely take Your Honour up on that advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Hartmann, are you comfortable there, or do you wish to come further forward? Because you're still far away from counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It's okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There has been, as is to be expected in a case of this sort, a number of exchanges back and forth. There have been areas of agreement and areas of disagreement. With respect to the question of admissions or identifying areas that are not in issue, I, on behalf of the Prosecution, forwarded a list of areas. My learned friend considered them carefully and returned a list of agreed areas, and for that I'm very grateful to him. So we have been able to narrow the issues down in terms of points that I thought were not in issue. My learned friend forwarded to me, I believe it was yesterday or the day before, a list of areas that he thought could be the subject of similar admissions. I hadn't seen a list or a description of areas that he was seeking agreement on, and as he quite accurately pointed out, at first blush I think that some of them can be the subject of admissions. Some of them I need a little bit of time, and I've indicated to him that I would get back to him on Monday. I need the weekend to consider that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you, Mr. MacFarlane. I think you will perhaps also discuss with Mr. Khan your availability or otherwise in relation to the information that he's -- other information he's trying to seek from you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- by way of a subpoena or in some other fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Well, he also raised the question today about what he referred to as chain of custody and provenance on some documents. Some of those documents are not going to be relied upon by the Prosecution, so I've questioned the relevance of chain of custody and provenance where I'm not seeking to any longer rely upon those, and so that's an area of discussion and perhaps disagreement; and some of the other documents for which he was seeking chain of custody or provenance were attached to the Registrar's initial initiating documents to the Chamber, so that's an area of discussion as well. Insofar as the question of an interview, it seemed to me that before I could properly respond to my learned friend on that question, I needed to have an understanding of the issues that the Chamber felt were properly before the Tribunal, before the Chamber, and that is the reason why I suggested that we await the decisions. All of those decisions have now been delivered, with reasons to follow. I think it's safe to say that the request to interview and to potentially call the opposing counsel is quite extraordinary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Keep them distinct, please. To interview is one thing; to call is another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. The short answer to the question from the Chamber is that, having regard to the decisions that have been made by the Chamber, I would like to consider the matter and will undertake to get back to my learned friend on Monday, on his request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Monday, or Tuesday, when we hand down the written decision on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes. It would be beneficial to have the reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, I understand that. En passant when you were discussing this matter, you mentioned something that I meant to raise in due course myself, namely, the question of agreed facts. It would be helpful for the Trial Chamber if we know exactly what these agreed facts are before we start -- before we start the trial because we, too, have to prepare. Thank you. Mr. MacFarlane and Mr. Khan, in the past weeks we read very carefully - Judge Moloto, obviously only in the last few days; he had to cope with the several hundreds of pages that we had already gone through, and I'm grateful for him having caught up so efficiently with us - we have gone through all the documentation, all the motions, and of course given them our utmost attention. One of the things that we had in mind mentioning today and which you have indirectly prompted, Mr. MacFarlane, by what you said a few minutes ago is the following: A few minutes ago you said: "Insofar as the question of the interview, it seems to me that before I could properly respond to my learned friend on that question, I needed to have an understanding of the issues that the Chamber felt were properly before the Tribunal, before the Chamber." We believe that the issues have been made clear, first, by our order in lieu of the indictment and, secondly, also by our decisions so far that relate to the matter. However, I have a question for both of you in preparation of the trial, and this is whether you have considered that the reference to the contents of the underlying protected documents, whether you have considered the reference to the contents of the underlying protected documents to be excluded from what is formulated in the form of a charge and the order in lieu of the indictment. And I am asking you this because this may not necessarily coincide with the Trial Chamber's understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I must confess. I don't fully understand the question. Perhaps I would be enlightened if I could have the Trial Chamber's understanding, and perhaps I could then either accept it or make submissions on that understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will repeat the question. In trying to understand the nature and the substance of the charges brought against your client in our order in lieu of the indictment, have you considered that the reference to the contents of the underlying protected documents to be excluded from the formulation adopted in that order?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I'm telling you this because if you do consider them to be excluded, then you might also need to consider that this might not coincide with the Trial Chamber's understanding of the order in lieu of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, our understanding, to the best of my knowledge and the best of my ability, has been detailed in our Defence brief, and I can refer Your Honours to that, if that's of any assistance. It's paragraph 9 of our Defence brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can read it. It's from the public version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 9 states: "The nature of the charges of Ms. Hartmann." And we wrote: "Ms. Hartmann is charged with disclosing the following facts: 1, the existence and date of the two impugned decisions; 2, the confidential character of these decisions; 3, the identity of the moving party and applicant; 4, the subject, namely the fact that protective measures were granted in relation to the documents." Your Honour, that was filed on the 15th of January. At the best of my recollection, there's been no comment on departure from my learned friend that that understanding has been incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, when I addressed this issue, I wasn't directing it only to you. I was also directing it to towards Mr. MacFarlane because we want to make sure -- we want to make sure that -- we want to make sure that you read from the part regarding the factual allegations supporting the charges contained in the order in lieu of the indictment the way we read them, and you have in one paragraph: "On the 10th of September, 2007, a book entitled "Paix et Chatiment," authored for publication by Florence Hartmann, was published by Flammarion, pages 121 to 122 of the book, in particular disclose information related to the decisions of the Appeals Chamber dated ..." and you have the two dates "... including the contents and purported effect of these decisions, as well as to the specific reference to the confidential nature of these decisions." You read the following paragraph, starting with: "On the 21st of January, 2008 ..." Again, at the end we have a reference to the two confidential decisions of the Appeals Chamber, dated, including the contents and purported effect of these decisions. Anyway, we are not going to say more. We felt it our duty to point this matter out to you before we hopefully start the trial on Thursday of next week, of the coming week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm most grateful for that question. I will say, because it's relevant to the due notice, fair notice aspect of this case, that our stated position in our pre-trial brief on the 15th of January was put verbatim by the Defence in our motion to -- for reconsideration, dated the 14th of January, and that's at paragraphs 14 to 18, and the Prosecutor, the Amicus Prosecutor in this case took no issue with it. In my respectful submission, given that we have a legitimate expectation that our understanding is correct, if it was not, surely being the diligent and experienced prosecutor that he is, issue would have been taken with it in the reply at the proper time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, in putting the question, I didn't ask you to perhaps consider whether your understanding of the charge tallies with that of Mr. MacFarlane. I put the question to make sure that both of you give a thought to what has been exchanged by way of motions and decisions so far and submissions and make sure that your understanding of the charges tally with the Trial Chamber's understanding of the charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in my respectful submission, perhaps not. Now that an Amicus Prosecutor has been appointed, what's important, in my respectful submission, is the way the Prosecutor puts his case so that the Trial Chamber has the distance and objectivity and detachment available to decide the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: So what's important is now the Prosecutor, how he's put his case, not, with the greatest of respect, what's in the mind of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Do you wish to comment, Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I think at this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone, and briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. I certainly -- the Chamber has asked counsel to direct their minds to this particular point, and certainly, I intend to do that and have done that. But the matter having been highlighted by the Chamber, I think it's incumbent on both counsel to give perhaps further attention to the issue raised. There does appear to be a triangulation of issues here, that is, the order in lieu of indictment, the contents of the book, and the underlying documents to the extent that they're referred to in the order in lieu of indictment. So I certainly intend to review the comments of the Chamber and direct my mind sharply to the points that have been raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to be difficult, but whilst it always behoves counsel to give the greatest respect and attention to any comment emanating from the Bench, I do put my learned friend on notice that any departure now at this late stage, on the eve of a scheduled trial, in my respectful submission will amount to a shifting of the goalposts and one that we on behalf of Ms. Hartmann will take the very strongest exceptions to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Now, the next item on the agenda is any other matter that the parties wish to raise. Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is, in fact, and it unfortunately focuses on the possibility of having the trial next week. I'll cut to the chase. In our respectful submission, that will not be feasible. The reason for that is that a number of requests are pending. We have sought at the beginning of January waiver from -- immunity from New York from the Secretary-General of the United Nations in relation to certain court staff, both in the Prosecution and in the Registry. We have not received that waiver as yet. We have also -- that's in relation to a Prosecution witness that will be called by the Amicus Prosecutor, in relation to a Registry member of staff, and also in relation to another Registry member of staff that we say may well be critical to the understanding of this case. Your Honour, that Registry member of staff was interviewed by the Amicus Prosecutor and was very heavily relied upon in the submissions that went before Your Honours and were relied upon when the order in lieu of an indictment was issued. Now, Your Honour, two issues arise. It is my instructions that my client made a formal complaint against that individual while she was a staff member. We have asked the Registry for disclosure of that complaint because it is our position that Your Honours would not want a criminal process to be used as a means of settling old scores because of personal enmity that may have existed. Now, Your Honours, we have addressed that to the Registrar, and we were told yesterday by the Acting Registrar that we will need an order of the Court. Your Honour, that is one matter that is pending, an application to Your Honours that the Registrar be ordered to give us information. I'm not going to belabour that point. It will be the subject of a written motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The second is, we have sought a wave of immunity so we can speak to that individual. Now, Your Honours, that person is not being called by the Prosecution, it is true, but in my submission that is not the end of the story. Your Honours, we, of course, are operating in a unique environment in which Your Honours have crafted rules and will give life to those rules through the statute and international human rights standards. But posing for a moment by way of analogy, in England and Wales, albeit a common law system, it is quite common that any witness who's name is on the back of an indictment at committal must be available to the Defence. My learned friend, in my submission, has relied upon a witness which was the catalyst in many respects, the foundation, even, for the order in lieu of indictment being issued. We want to speak to that individual, and we have performed -- we've conducted ourselves properly, in our submission. We have sought waiver of that person's immunity, in accordance with the applicable law. Your Honour, in addition, there are a number of documents that we need translating. Now, we received, I think it was yesterday or the day before, some response from the CMSS -- CLSS, and they very understandably said that the documents we had given were too copious. Your Honours, we are in -- some of them are in B/C/S. In fact, the client at the moment, Ms. Hartmann, is going through them to focus on those documents which we do need to tender into evidence, and when we've whittled it down to what is most required, we will resubmit it to the court translation system. Your Honour, so that's another matter why we say we are not going to be available for trial. Your Honour, in addition to the Prosecution witness, we've had great cooperation from the Deputy Prosecutor, and he's tried to assist us. But there are some evidential matters that we have sought, and we received a letter yesterday from the Deputy Prosecutor. He has sent us even e-mails over the weekend to all our responses, and we go on record for thanking him for the prompt cooperation. But, Your Honours, those evidential matters have not been settled as yet. We are looking for information that we say is germane to the case, that is relevant to Your Honours, and has to be brought to Your Honours' attention. Your Honour, the final matter is the most awkward, and it's one that I am actually loathe to raise, but sometimes it's counsel's duty to make and unsavoury or unwelcome or unwanted submissions. Your Honours, I will be filing in this case an application next week for the disqualification of Your Honour, the Presiding Judge, and His Honour Judge Orie. Your Honour, that is not to say that we think there is any impropriety, there is anything other than the highest professional standards and impartiality. You are, all three of you, judges of the very highest integrity and great experience, and it's a privilege appearing before all three of you. However, on the facts of this case, we say that there is a real apprehension of bias because the rules as they have been applied have not been properly followed in the sense that contamination has taken place between the Bench -- inadvertent, no doubt, but between the Bench and the Amicus Prosecutor. Your Honour, only yesterday we received in the filing of the Amicus Prosecutor, which, incidentally, it has the unfortunate aspect, again, it's ones of the problems we face in which he's giving evidence in a filing. In the filing, he refers to conversations with a court officer, and it's reliance upon the conversation with court officer that certain things were done which are challenged by the Defence. Now, Your Honour, that has at least two unfortunate consequences. It puts the particular court officer assisting the Bench in the invidious and unwelcome position of being a potential witness because these issues are in dispute by the witness. Secondly, in our respectful submission, the whole purpose of the rules, when Your Honours adopt this procedure, is to ensure the transparency of the process and the integrity of the Bench. In our respectful submission, 77(3), the summary procedure, the power of the Court itself to spontaneously investigate, is not at all apposite for this case. It surely was conceived by the drafters to be confined when there is contempt in facio curia, contempt in the face of the course. This case quite plainly applies to ex facio curia contempt, an allegation of contempt outside the face of the court. But, Your Honour, where there's been no paper trail, no filings, but on the basis of phone calls, authorisations given to disclose that which is confidential, authorisations to speak to individuals that on paper have been prohibited, very real questions arise. Now, Your Honours, under Rule 15, the normal procedure would be that we would file to Your Honour, as Presiding Judge, and Your Honour as the Presiding Judge would consult with the Judge whose recusal is sought, and it could go to the President. Your Honour, I will put this in the motion, but my application would be to file to Your Honours and that Your Honour pass the whole file to the President to determine this matter. If there's no merit in our fear that a reasonable bystander acquainted with the facts, that the origin of this came from the Registry, that there has been this -- the way the amicus has been appointed and conducted himself, if it's baseless, of course, it will be decided, and Your Honours will remain seized of the matter. But if there is merit in our submission, it's only right and proper that the integrity and the reputation and -- well-deserved reputation of the Bench of this Court and this Tribunal be protected by that danger being removed. That is another reason, in my submission, why the trial date for next week should be vacated, in addition to the evidentiary concerns that we have raised. Your Honour, in this case, when assessing the balancing exercise between the fair-trial rights of Ms. Hartmann and the appearance of justice, it is pertinent and appropriate, in my respectful submission, to note that there is no cost, financial cost, to international justice by a delay, by time being given to the Defence to do that which the Defence say is required. Your Honours, Ms. Hartmann, of course, appears voluntarily, without a warrant. She's not in custody. There is no live case. There is no victim as such that requires closure. In those circumstances, in the balancing of your discretion, I would ask, notwithstanding the fact that Your Honours quite clearly have got a time line, quite clearly anticipate and are ready to hear this matter next week, that the trial date be vacated to allow us to properly and without rush - without rush - seek notice of appeal, seek leave to appeal the various decisions which we seek to impugn, and also to get the evidence that we require from Prosecution witnesses, from the Registry, and the documents we require, to get the translations we require, and in addition to file an application under Rule 15 so that this matter can be settled once and for all. Your Honour, if it's without merit, you will remain seized; if it has merit, it's only right and proper that the President can appoint, under Rule 15(3) Judges that have not been touched by the investigation, that have not been part of the investigation, and the appointment of the Amicus Prosecutor to investigate the matter and then decide whether or not the Defence application has merit or otherwise. But, Your Honours, in those circumstances, a rush to judgement next week really does not cause -- does not serve, in my humble and very respectful submission, the course of justice. Your Honours, those are the issues I wish to raise that I think are most -- most directly impinge upon today's hearing and the prospect of trial next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Mr. MacFarlane, do you wish to respond or to comment on any of the submissions that Mr. Khan has made?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I'll endeavour to comment briefly on most, if not all of the points. Some of them are new to me, and I'll endeavour to assist the Chamber, to the extent that I can. With respect to the -- what I believe was the first point concerning a witness located within the Registry of this Tribunal for which immunity was being sought, it was suggested that the evidence or the comments of that individual were relied upon heavily in the proceedings leading up to the order in lieu of indictment. I would suggest that the Chamber take a look again at the report because the report makes it clear that the final recommendation and conclusion that was put forward to the Chamber was based entirely on the words -- the alleged words of the accused herself, and that was made clear in the report. Secondly, the documents which are sought for translation, which were described as too copious, I don't have any information. I haven't heard anything about that before, so I'm not in a position to comment on that. All I know is that in my experience with that division of the Tribunal, they are very efficient and very effective, and I'm sure that they will move as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can skip that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. The third point, as I have it recorded, concerned the witness from the Office of the Prosecutor, and there is reference to some evidentiary matters. I have a little bit of knowledge on that. I understand that discussions are in process, and if I can assist my learned friend in any way, I'd be happy to try to assist. So I simply put that forward as an offer to him. With respect to the last point which my learned friend described as an awkward one and a proposed motion for disqualification, and he referred to it as a contamination which has arisen in this case, I feel it important for me to describe and emphasise the checks and balances that have been in place right from the beginning. The Chamber was entitled to move directly to an order in lieu of indictment without any sort of investigation if the Chamber so desired, and that has been done before. But rather than moving in that fashion, the Registrar, as the officer in charge and as a neutral party, prepared a document of concern and forwarded it to the Chamber. The Chamber, in a neutral and detached way, reviewed the Registrar's assessment and felt that there is at least some semblance of concern and decided to arrange for the appointment of a neutral and an independent amicus curiae, in fact, someone from 5.000 miles away who had absolutely no connection to the Tribunal, to the accused, or anyone else. So there is a third layer of safeguards that were put in place. That report then went forward to the Chamber. The Chamber, in a neutral and detached way, reviewed that report and arrived at the conclusion that, yes, there was some basis for concern, and issued the order in lieu of indictment. So we have a situation where the Statute, the rules, and the practice direction all at least contemplate varying layers of safeguards and protections, and that worked. That worked in this particular case. There was those layers of safeguards, there were checks and balances at each stage, and we are now in a situation where the order in lieu of indictment was issued in August. There was an amended order in lieu of indictment in October, at the end of October. We have new counsel on the case. There have been a number of motions. The trial date has been set and protected now for quite a period of time. It seems to me that given that backdrop of safeguards and protections, and with the date being set and everything in motion, there's no basis on which to reconsider the composition of the Chamber, and it's my respectful submission that we are in a position to proceed to trial and have a neutral and detached assessment of the evidence based on the merits. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan and Mr. MacFarlane. Of course we have taken notes of all your submissions, Mr. Khan, and your submissions, Mr. MacFarlane. Obviously, the most important of these submissions is the last one relating to the intimated arrival of motion of disqualification. We enjoin you to file this motion with the utmost of celerity, please, and with your experience you know exactly why. You have given it a lot of importance. I'm sure it's the product of much thought, and equally, we want to take it as seriously as you propose it. I can assure you it's not the first time in our career that we have been challenged, and it's certainly not going to be the last time. So we will wait for this motion. We enjoin you to give it priority over everything else, please, and I'm sure -- I am sure that -- and I am sure that you will comply. You are two very qualified, experienced lawyers, and you shouldn't find difficulties on this. On the other issues that you raised, as much that one could say, I mean, some could be premature; some could be -- like, for example, the question of immunity, it could easily be solved at the end of the day by Monday morning for all that matters, or by Thursday for all that matters, or even Friday. And the translation issues, finishing or the availability of Prosecution documents, I think at the end of the day, if we put an effort we can find a solution to all these problems to your satisfaction, and whatever needs to be taken care of later on could be taken care of later on. But all this is predicated, of course, on the question of the expected motion of disqualification. We will also give priority to that and see how to dispose of it and when. Because of that, for the time being, obviously, we are not changing the schedule for the start -- for the commencement of trial. You should be prepared to start the trial on the 5th or on the 6th, but obviously we're on shifting ground. Much will depend on what will happen, what will happen. Also, also, because there is the other matter pending, namely, the question of certification, appeal certifications, which we have been given advance notice of. Now, we realise that there is no point in fixing a specific date for the filing of motions for certification of those decisions that have been decided orally today, with written reasons to follow. But the system -- the approach that we are going to adopt is the following: That we're going to divide the motions that have been decided into two categories - those that have already been decided up to yesterday, and for those, if you intend to seek certification for the purpose of appealing in relation to any one of them, you have until the end of the working day on Monday to file the motion, and you will have until Tuesday, the end of Tuesday, to reply, Mr. MacFarlane, or, rather, noon on Tuesday, noon on Tuesday, to reply. Let me finish, Mr. Khan, please. I will give you all the opportunity to -- we belong to the same system, so we know exactly how to deal with each other, with one another. The other motions, those -- there is one that we decided today, which is a minor motion. I don't know whether you will be seeking -- the one about the 65 ter list. But if you do intend to seek certification for that, you also have up until Monday. It's something which is not controversial, easy, and shouldn't create any problems. The other two, we are going to do our best, our level best, to come down with the written reasons by not later than Tuesday, by not later than Tuesday, and by "Tuesday," I mean the earliest possible on Tuesday. We will then, in the decisions themselves, shorten the time for the filing of motions for certification, and you will have an indication from now that it will be a very short time for the filing of such motions. Of course, by then we would have expected receipt of your motion for disqualification. So you will see that you are going to keep us very busy in the course of next week. I know this is no easy task for anybody, neither for us but certainly not for you, and we do appreciate that we are putting you and also Mr. MacFarlane, because he will have to respond in any case also within a matter of hours, under a lot of pressure. But one of the motions that we have decided today, namely, the stay of proceedings, is something that you will understand if we are going to proceed next week, this is not a matter that can be left for the week after to be decided as to whether there should be certification or not. In other words, whether we start next week or not will depend ultimately on our decision on the motion to stay the proceedings, whether we certify it for appeal purposes and our decision on disqualification, if we can decide that in time before the 5th of February because there is also that "if." Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you so much, and to Your Honours. Your Honour, the first issue, I'm very obliged by the very gracious manner in which the Bench dealt with the intimation regarding the Rule 15 application. Your Honour, in relation to the rest of it, in my submission, I do ask the Trial Chamber to be understanding of the realities of a trial process. I know there are at least two very experienced defence lawyers on the Bench that have practiced defence work prior to their elevation to the Bench. Your Honour, the reality is this, that I have, to the best of my ability, adumbrated the evidential hurdles that are yet to be overcome. Even if we obtained waiver from New York regarding important witnesses, we have to speak to those people. We have to interview them. We have to then analyse the evidential work product if we wish to call those individuals as witnesses. Your Honour, we can't -- in my submission, the Bench, to put it quite candidly, should be cautious about any appearance of unseemly haste to judgement in this matter, given that the accused is not in custody, that there are these real issues outstanding. It's very common in trial proceedings to vacate trial dates. It's not the end of the world to vacate a trial date when one is balancing that against the integrity of the process. Your Honours, we don't have information from the Registry. We don't have information and evidence from the Prosecutor. We have not yet got the waiver of immunity to interview witnesses. Your Honour, that has to be put on the scale as to the ability of the Defence to have a real process, a real shot at testing this evidence. If we are to get a real shot at testing the evidence and presenting to the Bench the real pitch of what underlies this matter, in my respectful submission, one has to vacate the hearing for next week. Your Honour, to seek to compress all these multifarious issues, expecting us to have some super-human skills, to respond to these motions, seek applications for leave to appeal, file Rule 15 motions, and try to scurry around and get evidence from the Registry that has provided personnel files for the Prosecution in Rule 33 submissions and is not providing it to us, the Defence, that may materially assist us, is to unnecessarily compress the course of justice into a gap that is unseemly. And, Your Honours, I do ask you to vacate the trial date because there are also issues of witnesses. We have five witnesses that we intend to call, and Your Honours, that will waste money, to get all these witnesses ready to come to court when we're not ready for trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, you should be ready for trial. When you took over from previous counsel, one of the conditions was your agreement to honouring the trial dates, and the trial dates of the 5th and the 6th of February weren't fixed last week. They were fixed a long time ago, prior to your arrival, and after due consultation with the previous lawyer and also your client because we have also in the course of arriving to this stage always taken into consideration the problems that -- and work exigencies, employment exigencies of your client. So there is no unseemingly haste at all. The dates were fixed a long time ago, and we have ourselves adjusted our timetable, court-scheduled sittings, accordingly to be able to start. Had there been unseemingly haste, we would have acted quite differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I clarify one point: Your Honour is quite correct that when I accepted the instructions in this case, I said that my appointment and the appointment of Mr. Guenal and the replacement of previous counsel would not be a cause of delay. Our appointment is not the cause of delay. Your Honour, the cause of delay -- if I could mention this issue. On the 30th of December, within a matter of days of our appointment, we contacted New York regarding waiver of immunity of our first witness, and, Your Honour, it continues: further letters on the 6th of January to New York, the 26th of January, 12th of January. Your Honour, we have not been dilatory. There are procedural safeguards when one is dealing with a bureaucracy and an international institution that is the United Nations, and there are consequences for dealing with that institution and respecting the privileges that are in place. Your Honour, one of our objections with our learned friend is the fact that he spoke to individuals - we've said it in our filings - he spoke to individuals, relied upon them in his submission without a wave of immunity. It would be rank hypocracy for me, then, to do that which I blamed opposing counsel for doing. Your Honour, I am ethnically in my view estopped from contacting these witnesses that are UN staff members without the permission of the Secretary General of the United Nations, and that is the delay, Your Honour, not my appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not going to comment on this, but what you have just raised, namely, that you've had contacts with New York, written once, twice, three times, et cetera, that could constitute one reason why the testimony of that particular witness might have to be delayed. But in itself, do you think it is -- or are you submitting that it should be a reason why the trial should not start at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am, because these are important witnesses. One must look, Your Honour, firstly, how many witnesses the Prosecution are calling, and then one must look, which of those witnesses do I wish to speak to? Your Honour, I hoped in the matter of course it's a matter of certification, but we were not given access to statements. Now we have a clear refusal, and a decision that my learned friend was entitled not to follow the normal practice that the OTP carries out and not give statements, of course, increases the burden upon me to know what the witness is going to say, and I am not satisfied with the summaries. So therefore, I have an option, which is to interview these witnesses. Now, in relation to many of these witnesses, already we have sought the waivers. So I think the only that's a public witness is Robin Vincent. I haven't sought any waiver for him. But Your Honour, for the other witnesses -- he's a public witness. They're all public, in fact, for the Prosecution. But, Your Honour, in relation to the staff members, of course I need waiver to be lifted. As I said, Your Honours, you have in good faith, of course, to decide the merits of this application. But when one is adjudging the balancing exercise, the right -- the fairness of the process and the rights of the Defence, simply the fact that a date has to be vacated seems a rather light consideration in the scheme of things, when a woman who has her good name in the scales, and this is a criminal Prosecution, when one is judging that -- Your Honour said on the first initial appearance, Your Honour said at the initial appearance, and I read the transcript carefully, when William Bourdon was then representing, Your Honour talked about the seriousness and the grave implications of these types of charges. Well, Your Honours, they are grave. They are grave for any individual, particularly somebody who has tried to work and assist international justice. In those circumstances, not to allow -- effectively allow the Defence to do what we say, as professional members of the bar, we are required to do is unfortunate. And, Your Honour, when one is exercising your discretion in deciding whether or not to -- I say to rush to judgement next week or to -- in a very balanced and sober and impartial manner step back, allow these motions to be decided, allow us to get responses and interview these witnesses, I think it's - to use an American expression and perhaps a Canadian one - it's a no-brainer. Your Honour, it's my very sincere submission that you consider vacating the date for practical purposes. As I said, there are consequences of witnesses. It is my application, and I have nothing more to add, Your Honour. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. We will, of course, take into consideration your submission, but unless you hear from us to the contrary, for the time being the appointment stands. Of course, there are many ifs and buts because many things have -- a lot of water has passed under the bridge since this morning, and we have to take that into account as well. I mean, I can assure you that the three of us are very sober and reasonable in our approach, and I won't say more than that. In the meantime, please, again, once more, I enjoin you to come up with the most important motion of all that we have to give, like you should, absolute priority to. Thank you. Is there any other matter that you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One suggestion I would like to make, since the time factor has assumed quite an importance and it is definitely our wish to lessen the burden on everyone. You know what the system is like here. You file a motion and by the time it gets to us or to the other party, it takes time, and that is counter-indicated in the present circumstances. But it has to happen. What I'm asking you to do, both of you, is that when you have filings - and you will have in the coming days, both initiating motions and responses - I would like you to exchange courtesy copies with each other and also with our senior legal officer. That will reduce the time that we will need to take stock of what is being submitted and will put everyone in a better position. I hope -- I can only rely on your cooperation on this, and I am sure that coming from the jurisdictions that you come from, you will find no problems in extending to us and to each other this courtesy. Thank you. Is there anything else you would like to raise? Mr. MacFarlane? Do you wish to disqualify us as well? We'll give you the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. There is only one issue, and it may well be that given the various issue currents that are floating around that it's impossible to determine at the moment, but I find myself in the position of appearing on behalf of the Prosecution and also being listed as a witness on behalf of the Defence, and at some point that will have to be determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to prepare for the trial, to be preparing as a witness and to prepare for an interview at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not our intention to put the cart before the horse. I mean, we'll wait and come -- decide that issue, if it arises at all, in due course. So let's not deal with matters that can still wait. Anything else? No. So I thank you all coming and for the practical approach that you have taken within the limited circumstances in which you can operate, both of you, and we will hear from you and you will hear from us, of course, in the course of next week. Thank you. The Status Conference is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 4.56 p.m.
